analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to hold capital reserves against off-balance-sheet shell entities they sponsor.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Financial Services Committee, never got a vote, and drew zero cosponsors before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal banking regulators to set capital standards — including leverage limits — for "special purpose entities," the shell vehicles banks set up to move assets like loans off their balance sheets. Banks sponsor these entities to hold securitized loans, but before the 2008 crisis they often carried little or no capital, so losses there could gut the parent bank without warning. The bill told regulators to treat the vehicles more like banks themselves whenever the vehicle's failure would significantly hurt the sponsoring bank.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank depositors and taxpayers, who ultimately absorb losses when an undercapitalized bank fails. By requiring sponsoring banks to stand behind their off-balance-sheet vehicles with real capital, the bill would have reduced the chance that hidden losses elsewhere in a bank's structure surprise regulators and trigger another bailout. Bank regulators would also gain a clearer statutory mandate to police these vehicles.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each federal banking agency to write capital standards — a leverage limit and a risk-based capital requirement — for special purpose entities sponsored by the banks it regulates, mirroring the standards that apply to banks themselves.

Applies to any vehicle whose finances are so intertwined with its sponsoring bank that the vehicle's failure would significantly hurt the bank, directly targeting the off-balance-sheet structure that let bank losses build up out of regulators' sight before the 2008 crisis.

Lets agencies add whatever extra capital measures they decide are needed to keep these vehicles from becoming undercapitalized, and directs the agencies to define 'special purpose entity' with the securitization vehicles — trusts that hold transferred loans, issue securities against them, and pass cash flows to investors — squarely in view.

analysis.who_pays: Large insured banks that sponsor special purpose entities would have had to hold more capital against those vehicles, tying up funds they currently keep free. Some of that cost could flow through to borrowers as somewhat more expensive securitized credit, such as mortgages packaged into securities.

drawbacks.text: Forcing securitization vehicles to hold bank-style capital would make securitization more expensive for banks, and some of that cost would likely reach ordinary borrowers through pricier credit — securitization is how many mortgages and other loans get funded.

The bill leaves its most important term, 'special purpose entity,' to be defined later by the banking agencies jointly, and requires bank-conforming standards only 'to the extent practicable' — so its real strength would depend entirely on how regulators wrote the rules.

It is a narrow fix: it addresses capital only for vehicles sponsored by insured depository institutions, not the broader shadow-banking system, and it was introduced after regulators and accounting rulemakers were already pushing many such vehicles back onto bank balance sheets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but modest: banks would tie up more capital against vehicles they had used to keep risk off their books, and credit funded through securitization could cost somewhat more. Against that, the bill targeted a specific, demonstrated route to bank failure and taxpayer bailouts, and gave regulators flexibility on how far to push. It was a narrow, reasonable post-crisis safeguard — and it never received even one cosponsor or a committee vote, so it was never seriously weighed on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on June 2, 2009, seven months after the peak of the financial crisis, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No other member of the House cosponsored it, no hearing or markup is recorded, and the action history shows nothing after the committee referral.
The bill never received a committee or floor vote and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks that sponsored off-balance-sheet special purpose entities are better off: they never had to hold capital against those vehicles, and the deadline for new requirements passed with the bill's death.

for.name: Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other member signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled action on the bill during a Congress that was actively rewriting financial regulation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote and never drew a cosponsor from either party, so no partisan split ever formed; the only recorded supporter was its Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: Banks used sponsored special purpose entities to keep loans and risk off their balance sheets and outside capital requirements. The bill would have forced capital reserves against any vehicle whose failure would significantly hurt the sponsoring bank, directly cutting into that practice.

Vehicles that hold securitized loans would have faced leverage limits and risk-based capital rules, raising the cost of packaging loans into securities. Securitization does fund credit for ordinary borrowers, so tighter rules could modestly shrink or reprice that credit even as they make the system safer.
